reviews.one_line_contribution: A generalizability-theory audit of self-editing agent memory that measures how much of a memory item's downstream utility is a stable item main effect versus item-by-query interaction, derives the probe budget the per-item assumption implies, and tests whether an item-level prune decision beats removing the same number of items at random on held-out episodes.
reviews.closest_prior_work: The proposal names MEMAUDIT (arXiv:2605.02199) as the closest work and correctly distinguishes it, but that is the wrong neighborhood. The real threat is the data-valuation literature the proposal barely touches: the point-removal benchmarking line (OpenDataVal, Data Banzhaf, and the Kwon/Jia-adjacent evaluations) has repeatedly shown that per-instance value scores are unstable across resampling and that removal by score frequently fails to beat random removal — which is P-1, P-2 and P-4 in a different substrate. The proposal cites only arXiv:2406.04606 from this cluster and dismisses it as 'fine-tuning data, no probe-budget derivation'; a reviewer who knows the valuation literature will read the contribution as a domain transplant with a G-theory wrapper. Second threat: the ICL demonstration-instability line (Lu et al. 2022 on order sensitivity; work showing demonstration utility is query-conditional). Memory items injected into context are demonstrations, so 'item x query interaction dominates the item main effect' is qualitatively pre-established there. Novelty then rests on the quantitative probe-budget derivation and the CI-gated prune rule, which is a thinner contribution than the abstract implies.
reviews.strongest_objection: The two headline numbers are close to guaranteed by the chosen budget rather than by the phenomenon, so the audit cannot separate 'item value is unstable' from 'this study lacks resolution.' (a) P-3 — 'fewer than 10% of items have a 95% CI excluding zero' — is stated as the sharpest number in the paper, but Measurement and Noise Control concedes the per-item detectable effect at ~85 binary observations is ~±20 accuracy points. No one, including the curation papers under attack, believes a single item in a 120-item bank moves episode accuracy by 20 points. So P-3 is an arithmetic consequence of choosing 85 observations per item; it would come out the same in a world where every item had a perfectly stable +3-point effect. (b) P-4 — 'P1 - P2 within ±4 points, CI covering zero' — sets an equivalence band that is plausibly wider than the entire memory effect in this setup. The precheck gates only on ≥8% instance-level *disagreement* (churn), not on any net effect, and the track's own prior result is that a full bank fixed zero and broke six or seven items, i.e. a net effect of roughly a point. Removing 12 of 120 items cannot move an 800-instance paired comparison by 4 points under any hypothesis about item value, so the predicted null arrives regardless of whether the curation literature's premise is true. P3 does not rescue this: it is a transfer ceiling estimated on the same mismatched probe distribution, not an in-sample bound on how much *any* 12-item prune could move the metric. A second, independent version of the same problem: the item x query variance component is what P-1 hinges on, and the proposal never states how many distinct probe instances the 3,000 episodes cover. With 120 items and ~10,500 item-appearances, if the probe set is a few hundred instances then almost every (item, query) cell has zero or one binary observation, and item x query variance is not separably identified from Bernoulli residual — the 600-episode second-seed replicate only re-runs whole episodes and does not fix cell-level identification for the other 2,400. A headline decomposition whose largest component may be unidentified is not a decomposition.
reviews.what_would_fix_it: Three concrete changes, in order of importance. (1) Add an in-sample detectability ceiling: fit item effects on the held-out test set itself and prune the 12 worst, reported as an oracle arm. If even the test-fitted prune moves under 4 points, the paper has shown its outcome measure cannot resolve any 12-item decision, and the honest finding becomes a measurement-resolution result rather than a claim about item value — still publishable, but a different paper. If it moves well above 4 points while P1 does not, the transfer claim becomes real and decisive. (2) Report the total headroom the ±4-point band is being judged against: a no-memory arm and a full-bank arm on the same 800 paired instances, with the net delta and the fix/break decomposition. Equivalence bands must be calibrated to the phenomenon, not to the sample size. (3) Re-express P-3 relative to what is achievable: report the fraction of items whose CI excludes zero alongside the fraction that *could* exclude zero under a plausible true-effect distribution (e.g. simulate items with stable effects of 2, 5, 10 points at the same budget). Additionally, state the probe-set instance count and the expected observations per (item, query) cell, and either add cell-level replication or drop the item x query component in favour of a directly estimable stable-versus-total ratio. Finally, either align the probe injection distribution with deployment top-k (probe by swapping one retrieved item for its rank-k+1 successor, which is the actual prune counterfactual) or reframe the estimand explicitly as marginal-over-random-subsets and stop calling P1 vs P2 decisive.
reviews.missing_baseline: Two. First, an in-sample/oracle prune fitted on the held-out test set itself (distinct from P3, which is fitted on the full probe set and inherits the same distribution mismatch) — without it, a null on P1 vs P2 is indistinguishable from the metric having no resolution at the 12-item scale, and the paper's own Risk 4 cannot be discharged. Second, an empty-bank / no-memory arm in Phase 3. Given the track's prior finding that memory was net harmful, the practically relevant comparator is 'turn memory off', and P9 (tune k on a dev split) may simply select k=0, in which case the constructive corollary 'budget control dominates curation' silently reduces to 'do not use memory' — a very different recommendation that the current condition set cannot distinguish or report.
reviews.preprint_collision: The check is unusually honest about process — it states 14 queries, a single pass, a blocked second round, and names the specific scenario (a random-removal ablation buried in a curation preprint) that would gut the headline. That candour is worth credit. But it searched the wrong neighbourhood thoroughly and the right one not at all. Every cluster swept is agent-memory-side (A-MAC, SAGE, MEMAUDIT, GovMem, EDV, Memory-R1, A-MEM, PlugMem); the two literatures that actually threaten the claim are absent. (i) Data-valuation benchmarking, where 'per-instance scores are unstable under resampling' and 'value-ranked removal does not beat random removal' are established results with published point-removal protocols — the proposal touches this cluster with one citation (arXiv:2406.04606) and waves it off on substrate grounds, which is precisely the move a reviewer will refuse. (ii) ICL demonstration sensitivity, which already establishes qualitatively that demonstration utility is query-conditional rather than a property of the demonstration. Neither absence is a hard collision — I can name no preprint that runs this exact variance decomposition on an agent memory bank — but a novelty claim resting on a single-pass search that never queried the field where the same negative result is textbook is not established novelty. The residual-risk paragraph should be extended to cover these clusters, and the related work should argue the transplant is non-obvious rather than pretending the source result does not exist.

reviews.one_line_contribution: It applies a datamodels-style randomized-injection design plus a generalizability-theory variance decomposition to agent-memory items in order to measure, rather than assume, how much of an item's downstream utility is a stable item main effect versus item-by-query interaction, and then tests whether a curation decision made on that estimate transfers to held-out episodes against a bank-size-matched random-removal control.
reviews.closest_prior_work: Two things converge on it. (a) arXiv:2406.04606 ("Helpful or Harmful Data? Fine-tuning-free Shapley Attribution") already does the core reliability move — sign-instability of per-instance value scores under resampling — and the proposal's own split-half/sign-agreement analysis is that same test with a different object. The proposal's honest delta is the G-theory probe-budget derivation and the curation-transfer test, which is real but narrower than the framing ('item value is not an item property') implies. (b) The ICL demonstration-sensitivity literature (Lu et al. 2022 on prompt ordering, Zhao et al. 2021, and the influence-based selection papers the proposal cites) has made 'demonstration value is strongly context-dependent' close to received wisdom; a reviewer will ask what is surprising about item x query dominating for a demonstration-slot item. MEMAUDIT (arXiv:2605.02199) threatens the framing rather than the measurement — it has already published the conclusion ('value is combinatorial, score against a package oracle') that the proposal's P-1 is designed to support, so the paper risks being read as the appendix that justifies a design choice someone else already shipped. It does not fully scoop, because MEMAUDIT reports no variance components, no budget derivation, and no held-out transfer test.
reviews.strongest_objection: The decisive experiment may have a ceiling below its own minimum detectable effect, which makes the headline null uninformative. The precheck gate only requires that the memory agent differ from the no-memory agent on 8% of instances *in either direction* — that is a churn gate, not an effect-size gate, and it is satisfied by a bank whose net accuracy contribution is zero. Phase 3 then removes 12 of 120 items and asks McNemar, whose stated MDE is ~3.8 points, to adjudicate P1 vs P2. If the entire full-bank-vs-no-memory net effect is ~1-2 points (which the track's own prior results suggest: zero fixes, six-to-seven breaks), then no 10% prune of that bank can plausibly move accuracy by 4 points, and P-4's predicted null is guaranteed by construction rather than by the instability of item value. P3 is offered as the ceiling bound, but if P3 - P0 is also inside the noise band, the paper cannot distinguish 'item value is unestimable' from 'this bank has no item-level headroom in this environment', and every downstream recommendation collapses. A second, independent objection compounds it: P-5 is entailed by P-3 through attenuation. If fewer than 10% of items have posteriors excluding zero, the shrunken posterior used as the correlation target is mostly noise, so |Spearman| < 0.25 for every proxy is an arithmetic consequence of the measurement's own unreliability and says nothing about whether A-MAC's or SAGE's signal is valid. Declaring a whole family of published signals invalid on that basis is the sentence an area chair will circle. Third, the estimand is mismatched to the target: effects are estimated marginal over a uniform k~U{1..6} draw from the retriever's top-20, but curation methods operate on items that will be injected by top-k retrieval. A small query-marginal main effect relative to item x query interaction is precisely the regime a retriever exists to exploit, so low reliability of the marginal quantity does not by itself indict conditional, retrieval-aware curation.
reviews.what_would_fix_it: (1) Replace the churn-based precheck with a headroom gate: before committing 8,800 transfer episodes, compute from Phase 1 the best achievable subset-selection gain (oracle prune evaluated in-sample on probe data) and pre-register that the transfer test only runs, and only carries the claim, if that oracle gain exceeds the 3.8-point MDE; otherwise re-scope to a bank or environment with measurable item-level headroom, or raise held-out n. (2) Estimate item effects under two injection distributions - the uniform top-20 probe and a deployment-matched top-k conditional - and report reliability separately for each, so the claim addresses the estimand curation methods actually use. (3) Break the entailment between P-3 and P-5 by reporting disattenuated correlations and an explicit reliability ceiling on the maximum attainable |Spearman| given the measured split-half reliability; state in advance that a proxy correlation below that ceiling is uninformative rather than a refutation of the proxy. (4) Fix identifiability: items only ever appear on queries where they reach the retriever's top-20, so item and query are confounded and the crossed p x i design that the G-coefficient formula assumes does not hold; add a fraction of probe episodes with injection drawn uniformly over the entire 120-item bank to restore connectedness, and report the variance decomposition on that connected subdesign. (5) Add k=0 to the held-out arms (see missing baseline). (6) With 120 items, split-half rho carries a +/-0.17 CI, which cannot separate 0.35 from 0.45; either enlarge the bank or state the reliability finding as an interval claim rather than a threshold claim.
reviews.missing_baseline: A no-memory (k=0) arm on the 800 paired held-out instances. The paper's constructive corollary is that the injection budget, not item identity, is the decision variable - and k=0 is the endpoint of that budget. Given the track's own prior finding that full-bank injection fixed zero items and broke six to seven, it is entirely possible that k=0 beats P0, P1, P4 and P9, which would make the whole item-value audit moot and reframe the paper. Running it only in a 150-instance precheck is not enough. Two lesser omissions a reviewer will also raise: a positive-selection arm (keep only the top-12 estimated items, bank size matched by a random-12 control) - pruning the bottom decile of a 120-item bank is the weakest possible test of whether the estimates carry signal, since it manipulates 10% of the bank at the tail where the estimates are noisiest; and prune-by-retrieval-frequency, which is the cheapest deployable heuristic and appears only as a Phase-4 correlation, never as a paid condition.
reviews.preprint_collision: Above the median for this kind of submission and clearly not fabricated boilerplate: it names nine-plus specific arXiv IDs, distinguishes targets from collisions, absorbs GovMem's signal as a proxy rather than dismissing it, and states the exact scenario that would gut the headline (a random-removal appendix ablation in a recent curation preprint). It also declares that only a single pass ran because a second was tool-blocked, which is the right disclosure. But it is thin in a way that matters for this particular paper: the search covered the memory-curation literature, not the paper's own methodological core. Generalizability theory and item-response theory have already been imported into LLM and NLG evaluation for exactly this purpose - decomposing rater/item/instance variance and deriving how many observations a reliable ranking needs (the IRT-for-benchmarks and tinyBenchmarks-adjacent line, and the LLM-as-judge reliability work) - and none of it appears anywhere in the Related Work or the collision check. The author flags 'generalizability theory applied to LLM evaluation' as an uncovered query and then proceeds as if the gap were harmless; it is the one gap that could turn the methodological contribution into a straightforward transfer of an existing recipe to a new object. The OpenReview 2026/2027 sweep is likewise missing, which matters when the direct targets are 2026 workshop-track papers whose authors are plausibly running the random-removal control right now. Verdict: no named collision, but novelty is established only against the curation literature, not against the measurement literature the paper's method comes from.

reviews.one_line_contribution: A generalizability-theory audit of agent-memory curation: randomize which bank items are injected, decompose realized episode-level item value into a stable item main effect vs item-by-query interaction vs decoding noise, derive the probe budget a reliable per-item ranking would require, and test on held-out instances whether pruning 'identified harmful' items beats removing the same number at random.
reviews.closest_prior_work: Two, and the proposal underweights one of them. (a) 'Helpful or Harmful Data? Fine-tuning-free Shapley Attribution' (arXiv:2406.04606) is the closest methodological threat, not merely a spiritual cousin: it already establishes the template that per-instance value scores are not sign-stable under resampling, which is the same negative-reliability story. The proposal's delta is a domain transplant (fine-tuning data -> injected memory items) plus off-the-shelf G-theory machinery and a random-removal transfer control. That is a real delta, but it is an increment on an existing critique rather than a new kind of claim, and the novelty score reflects that. (b) MEMAUDIT (arXiv:2605.02199) already asserts that memory value is set-level rather than per-item and builds an evaluation protocol on it; the proposal's honest position -- 'we supply the number MEMAUDIT presupposes' -- is exactly the position a reviewer reads as 'measures the constant in someone else's already-published qualitative claim'. Datamodels (Ilyas et al. 2022) supplies the estimator wholesale, so no methodological novelty is claimed there. Nothing here is scooped outright, but the conceptual headline is pre-owned and the statistics are borrowed; what remains genuinely unclaimed is the probe-budget derivation and the cross-proxy validity sweep in Phase 4.
reviews.strongest_objection: Two-part, and the first is not fixable with more compute. (1) PREMISE MISMATCH. The paper's target -- 'every curation method presumes an individual item has a stable estimable utility' -- is not what A-MAC, SAGE, EDV, AutoManual or Memory-R1 actually assert. They assert that a heuristic write/admit policy improves aggregate end-to-end performance. That claim survives intact even if per-item utility ranking is completely unreliable, exactly the way a noisy-but-biased filter can raise average quality without ranking any individual instance correctly. So P-2's headline comparison -- 'the generalizability formula implies >800 observations per item, one to two orders of magnitude above what A-MAC/SAGE/Memory-R1 spend per item' -- is a category error: those systems never claimed to rank items by realized downstream utility, and holding them to a ranking-reliability standard they never asserted is the kind of framing an AC calls a strawman. P5 and P6 partially rescue this by testing the published signals operationally, but note that P5 repurposes an admission score, calibrated on a write-time stream with its own base rates, as a deletion ranking inside an already-deduped 120-item bank; calling that 'faithful' will be contested. (2) THE NULL IS CONFOUNDED WITH A LOW CEILING. Every primary prediction (P-1, P-3, P-4, P-6) is a predicted null, and their informativeness depends entirely on the bank having item-level effects large enough that unreliability, rather than absence of signal, explains the result. The precheck only demands >=8% instance-level DISAGREEMENT vs no-memory in either direction -- directionless churn, which the track's own prior results say this setup produces in abundance. Removing 12 of 120 items from a bank whose total net contribution may be a point or two cannot plausibly move accuracy more than a fraction of the design's own ~3.8-point MDE, so P-4 landing inside its +/-4 band is close to arithmetically guaranteed regardless of whether item value is stable. P3 is offered as the ceiling, but P3 is estimated under the same randomized-injection distribution (k~U{1..6} over top-20) that Risk Factor 3 concedes differs from top-k deployment, so a null P3 is equally consistent with 'the estimand we measured is not the estimand deployment needs.' Relatedly, P-3 -- billed as 'the sharpest single number in the paper' -- is a restatement of the sample size: the proposal itself states the per-item detectable effect at ~85 binary observations is ~+/-20 points, so almost no item can clear a 95% CI bar. Pre-registering that your own per-item analysis is underpowered is not a finding about memory. (3) IDENTIFICATION. The hierarchical model has random effects for item, query, item x query and seed, but no term for item x co-injected-set. Items are injected in subsets of 1-6, so interference between co-injected items (the very combinatorial structure MEMAUDIT posits) has nowhere to go but the item x query term and the residual -- which means P-1's headline, 'item x query interaction is the largest component and the stable main effect is under 20%', can be produced by item-item interference that is nothing to do with query dependence. Worse, because probe items only appear on queries where the retriever ranks them top-20, most item x query cells have exactly one observation, so item x query and residual are confounded in the classic G-theory way; the 600-episode second-seed replicate identifies pure decoding noise but not the item x query vs item x set split.
reviews.what_would_fix_it: (a) Restate the audited premise as what the literature actually claims -- 'these signals improve end-to-end performance' -- and let P5/P6 vs P2 carry the indictment, rather than the probe-budget comparison, which should be demoted to a remark about what a per-item ranking would cost. (b) Add an ORACLE prune fit on the held-out episodes themselves (item effects estimated in-sample on the 800 test instances, then applied to those same instances). This is the only condition that separates 'per-item value is unstable' from 'there is nothing in this bank to find' and from 'the probe injection distribution is the wrong estimand'; without it a null P1/P3 is uninterpretable. (c) Run an explicit no-memory arm on the same 800 held-out instances (800 episodes, cheap) and report every delta as a fraction of the full-bank-minus-no-memory effect. If that denominator is ~2 points, say so up front; the paper is then a scoped null about a bank with little to curate, and should be written as such. (d) Strengthen the precheck from directionless churn to a signed requirement (full bank must beat or trail no-memory by an amount exceeding the null-replicate band) -- churn is exactly what the track's prior work already reports. (e) Add a pairwise (second-order) presence term or a datamodel interaction term so that item x co-injected-set variance is estimated rather than absorbed into item x query, and report the variance decomposition with and without it; P-1 as currently stated is not identified. (f) Make the variance-component ratio, not the CI-count P-3, the headline number.
reviews.missing_baseline: The query-conditional gate. The proposal's own finding -- value lives in item x query, not in the item -- immediately implies the constructive alternative is context-conditional filtering: learn or score item-query harm at retrieval time and gate per query, which is precisely Open Question 3 of the track brief ('given a memory item and a query, can harm be predicted before injection?'). The plan has no such arm. Every prune condition (P1, P3, P4, P5, P6) and the recommendation (P9, tune k globally) are query-agnostic, so the constructive corollary 'controlling the bank-level injection budget dominates item-level curation' is established only against the strictly weaker family the paper has just declared misconceived. A reviewer will say the study measures that item main effects are small and then tests only interventions that use item main effects. Two further omissions: (i) no no-memory arm on the 800-instance held-out set, so no delta has a denominator; (ii) no oracle/in-sample-on-test prune to upper-bound what any item-level curation could achieve on the actual test distribution. Separately, P9 is described as 'tune k on a dev split' without stating whether k=0 is in the search space -- if it is and it wins, the paper's finding is about this bank, not about curation.
reviews.preprint_collision: Above average for this kind of submission and unusually self-aware -- it names the single scenario that would gut the headline (a random-removal control appearing as an appendix ablation in a recent curation preprint) and reports that none of the nine retrieved papers contains one. Credit for that. But it is explicitly a single-pass, 14-query search whose second round was blocked, and the gap it admits is the one that matters most: 'generalizability theory applied to LLM evaluation' went unsearched, and that is exactly the query most likely to surface a collision, since variance-components and G-coefficient analyses of LLM-judge and agent-eval reliability are an active 2026 preprint area. Also unsearched, and relevant: datamodel/context-attribution work applied to retrieved context in RAG, and per-demonstration attribution under resampling beyond the one Shapley paper cited. No OpenReview 2026 sweep. I cannot name a preprint that already makes this exact claim, and the proposal's dispositions of MEMAUDIT (arXiv:2605.02199) and GovMem (arXiv:2607.02579) are argued rather than asserted, which is the right standard. But 'the search I did not run is the one aimed at my own method' is a real weakness, not a neutral, and the MEMAUDIT relationship -- conceding that MEMAUDIT already assumes package-level value and positioning this work as supplying its missing constant -- compresses the novelty claim more than the proposal admits.
